topic.title: We panic about WhatsApp because it is the office
topic.claim: A false claim that WhatsApp would shut down in India spread fast because WhatsApp is no longer an app, it is how work and shops run.
topic.behaviour: A forwarded image said Meta would exit India, and people took it as news. Shopkeepers, clients and teams who run on one chat thread felt it at once.
topic.mechanism: When one app carries orders, payments and approvals, even a rumour feels like a threat to income. That makes it travel faster than a correction.
topic.group: small business owners, freelancers and office workers
topic.moment: Someone forwards 'WhatsApp is shutting down' and your first thought is the client group, not your family.

turn.believed: People fall for these claims because they are careless.
turn.actually: They react because one app has quietly become the place where their work lives.

topic.because: Dependence on a single tool makes any threat to it feel personal. A viral claim only has to land on that nerve.

proof.fact: A viral post shared an image reading 'We Will Exit India if Forced to Break Encryption'. The fact-check found no new announcement from Meta; the line goes back to 2024.

topic.payoff: Test: if WhatsApp went down tomorrow, count how many of your jobs would stop.
topic.send_to: The boss who runs the whole team on one WhatsApp thread.
real_details: The Department of Telecommunications has told messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram to keep accounts linked to an active SIM in the device, with a deadline of December 31, 2026.
topic.news_peg: Fact-check of the viral 'Meta will exit India' claim, 2026-10-23
topic.why_now: A new SIM-binding rule is also in the news, so the panic was easy to believe.

score.why: People panic about WhatsApp shutting because their work lives there, not because they're careless; the test is easy to run.

topic.villain: a single-app dependency that has quietly become critical infrastructure

history.cancelled: 2026-11-03: replaced by the owner's taste-test topics
